new_statements.rule_in_words: No source opened states where word stress falls. The only first-hand phonological sketch (Tucker & Bryan 1957, from Tucker's own fieldwork) describes Vanuma as a language with lexical and grammatical tone, contrastive vowel length in stems and a 'tendency to length on penultimate syllable' -- i.e. the familiar Bantu penultimate lengthening -- without using the word stress. The text above is stitched from overlapping Google Books snippets (the ellipses mark unseen words; 'I' and 'U' are the snippet's rendering of ɪ and ʊ), so it must be checked against the page before use.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any snippet or opened source.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level remark inside a three-page phonetics/tonetics sketch; examples are verb forms (màsámuɽa lvànùma 'I speak Vanuma'). Separately, Johnston 1902 (opened, p. 901) gives only a blanket convention for all his vocabularies, Libvanuma included: 'in the absence of any mark the accent falls on the penultimate syllable' -- not a Vanuma-specific claim. Rasmussen 2018 (opened) carries Vanuma segment and tone data but says nothing about Vanuma stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Tucker & Bryan's 'Vanuma' (Bvanuma, lí-vanumá) was recorded from speakers in Uganda's Amba territory (Bwamba, east of the Semliki) and is classed in vol. 1 (p. 127) as one dialect of a cluster whose other dialect is Nyali; Glottolog's vanu1242 point (0.94N 29.81E, DRC side of the Semliki) is the same variety, called Nyali-Tchabi / Nyali Tchabi by SIL (Morgan & Van Otterloo 2009; OLAC alt. name). Johnston 1902 labels his vocabulary 'Libvanuma or Lihuku', conflating Vanuma with Huku, which Glottolog lists as an alternative name of North Nyali (nyal1250). The Compendium snippet notes internal Vanuma dialects differing in tone.

sources.note: No descriptive (grammar/phonology/sketch) reference anywhere: Glottolog's most extensive description is Johnston 1904 (wordlist); OLAC/SIL know only the three 1995 survey items. Alternative names Bambutuku, Bvanuma, Livanuma, Nyali-Tchabi.

sources.citation: Johnston, Harry H. 1902. The Uganda Protectorate, vol. II. London: Hutchinson. (Glottolog ref 58624 cites the 1904 2nd ed.) Vocabulary no. 26 'Libvanuma or Lihuku', pp. 946-958; remarks pp. 896-897; 'Orthography employed in these vocabularies' p. 901.
sources.note: Only a blanket transcription convention on p. 901 covering all 35 vocabularies: "' shows where the accent falls: in the absence of any mark the accent falls on the penultimate syllable." Nothing Vanuma-specific about accent or tone; the Libvanuma column shows a few marked forms (e.g. 'Ukó'). Johnston treats Libvanuma and Lihuku as one language of the Mboga/Toba country west of the Semliki.

sources.citation: Rasmussen, Kent. 2018. A Comparative Tone Analysis of Several Bantu D30 Languages (DR Congo). PhD dissertation, University of Texas at Arlington (Linguistics & TESOL Dissertations 116).
sources.note: Vanuma [vau] figures only in the D30 segment inventories (Tables 3-5, nine vowels and consonants after Morgan & Van Otterloo 2009) and in the comparative cognate/tone tables of ch. 6-7 (e.g. Tables 30-41, 52); there is no Vanuma chapter and no statement about Vanuma stress ('stress' occurs only for Ndaka, p. 116). Vanuma data credited to Bakabukingi Bolanao William and Babote Rwabongo Gus- (p. xii) and workshop databases.
